results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The intro reader predicted all seven sections in the spec's order, the three kinds of evidence (Larkfield case, provider documentation with access dates, worked arithmetic) and the plain, directive tone.
33 of 33 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; the three callouts are aligned to nothing.

results.quote: So for each provider, write down five terms from its documentation: what can be read back by identifier, key retention, the version pin and its notice period, the webhook retry window and acknowledgement deadline, and the request limits.
results.finding: The paragraph holds the part synthesis (four edges, four incidents assumed a wider contract) and a separate course of action (write down five terms, then why the payment service holds the keys). The spec requires the takeaway and so-what in the conclusion but gives them no paragraph, so the draft, which may not add a unit, put them inside p31.

Every argument paragraph ties to S1 to S4; the request-log paragraph (When It Goes Wrong ¶3) ties to S1 and S4 only through recovery ('what did we send?'), which is thin but stated; p03, p04, p32 and p33 are structural.
3 figures (each with a caption saying what it shows), 5 tables and the quotations of every spec evidence item are introduced or followed by a sentence saying what they show.

32 of 32 declared boundaries (7 sections, the conclusion, 24 paragraphs) express the declared relationship. Weakest: the Credentials section opens on keys in general and picks up the review's first question only through 'reach' and 'refunds and payouts'.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Three Questions About One Morning ¶2
results.quote: And which limit applied, and where was it written? The key did no harm that day; it is here because the review found it in the same place as the limit, among the terms of the API that nobody had read.
results.finding: The first two questions are each followed by an answer; the third is followed by an aside about the key, with no answer and no word that the answer comes in the limits section. Both readers re-read to look for it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.4 (flow reader A, item 3.3)

results.draft_locus: Request Limits: Rate Limiting and Load Shedding ¶3
results.quote: Note the third row of the table: a batch that sends one kind of request meets the 25, not the 100.
results.finding: The sentence that explains the incident points at a row of a table the reader has not yet seen and closes a paragraph about what the documentation confirms; both readers read on to the table and came back.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.7 (flow reader A, item 3.4)

results.draft_locus: Request Limits: Rate Limiting and Load Shedding ¶5
results.quote: Both providers document the first design. Stripe documents the second ("a client-side token bucket rate-limiting algorithm") and the third.
results.finding: The prose speaks of the first, second and third design before the table that names them (React, Pace, Agree); one reader had to read the table and then re-read the paragraph. Reported by flow reader B (item 3.8) only.

results.draft_locus: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
results.quote: | Request logs | Request logs in Workbench (2024) and a log link on each error; per a support article, 31 days for GET requests and 15 months for other requests | API logs for thirty days (JSON requests only); a seven-day dashboard | Stripe shows what you wrote for longer; keep your own request log on both |
results.finding: The comparison table summarises request logs (and names Workbench) two sections before logs are introduced. The spec declares this row in p19 while its flow rationale says logs appear 'nowhere sooner' than the failure section, so the difficulty comes from the declared order.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.6 (flow reader A, item 3.5)

results.quote: This is the Phantom Payment in reverse: your system believes a payment failed when the provider never tried it.
results.finding: The failure-patterns callout defines the Phantom Payment as exactly this case ('a request refused for volume was recorded as a failed payment, although the provider had never tried it'), so 'in reverse' has nothing to reverse; both readers went back to compare the two.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.1 (flow reader A, item 3.9)

results.quote: Across this part, every protection the API offers turns out to have an edge.
results.finding: From this sentence one long paragraph inside the chapter summary changes scale to the whole part and packs in four edges, four incidents, four Keel decisions and a list of five terms (five after four; 'key retention' first read as API-key retention). Both readers re-read it. The position between the take-away lists and the questions, apart from the hand-off, and the content of the one unit are the spec's.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.13 (flow reader A, item 3.8)

results.finding: All terms on does_not_know (restricted and publishable key, API credential with roles, company and merchant account, sandbox, test card, load shedding, dunning, issuer) are defined at first use; Keel decisions, incident names and idempotency keys are in already_knows. 'Workbench' in the comparison table precedes its introduction; that is ruled under flow_is_followable (request-logs row).
Opens on the dated incident and states a disputable thesis in ¶2; none of the weak patterns.
No 'in conclusion', no rephrased-thesis ending, no sentimental appeal; the edge figures in ¶4 point to earlier chapters with links and are not new evidence.

What to Take Away ¶4 relates key retention, the webhook retry window, the version notice and the request rate as edges of one contract, names the four Larkfield incidents (Double Charge, Version Cliff, Silent Webhook, Renewal Wave) with K1, K7, K2 and K5, and says why it matters ('That is why the payment service holds the keys...'), before the hand-off to part-5.
'The 7,900 emails of the opening' in the author's synthesis, and the four incidents of the part opening in ¶4.

The cold reader said the run showed that code handles each shape and state, did not show issuer behaviour, latency or live limits, computed about 49 requests a second, compared it with Stripe's 25 per endpoint and 100 per account, said to agree a rate with Adyen, to pace client-side and to back off on 429 with the same idempotency key. Matches expected.

The cold reader chose a read-only restricted key (or an Adyen credential with only the needed roles), justified it by what a leak allows, and said the money-moving key exists in one place. Matches expected.

Stripe's 2017 design carries '(Evidence age: 9 years; the current system may differ.)' and ¶3 of Request Limits says what current documentation confirms, contradicts and does not confirm; 'Adyen publishes none of this for payments' and no limiter design 'I found in neither its documentation nor its engineering posts'; 'Adyen publishes no list of what its test environment cannot simulate.'
